title: Adaptive windowing and prioritized queue benchmark plan
content:
Summary:

This note lays out an experimental plan to evaluate two complementary scheduler strategies aimed at improving tail latency without sacrificing throughput: 1) adaptive windowing (dynamic observation-time windows for forming batches) and 2) prioritized request queues (lightweight per-tenant or per-route priority that influences batch formation order). The goal is to surface bottlenecks, quantify tradeoffs (cost/latency/fairness), and produce a clear rollout path for Canary in Redwood Dedicated and Hosted API environments.

Motivation and context:
- Current continuous-batching implementation uses fixed max_batch and fixed aggregation timeout per model family. This leads to suboptimal tail behavior for mixed workloads (short vs long seqs, interactive vs async).
- Previous notes (scheduler-batching-timeout-fairness-experiment-log, batching-policy-sensitivity-scratchpad) explored static param sweeps; we need adaptive strategies that react to request inter-arrival distributions.
- Instrumentation shows occasional CPU stalls in the batching loop and KV-cache hot keys correlating with p99 spikes. We need microprofiling plus algorithmic changes.

Hypotheses:
1) Adaptive windowing that shortens timeout under high arrival rates and lengthens it under low arrival rates will reduce p99 while keeping average latency stable.
2) Prioritized queues that allow small interactive requests to bypass long-transaction-heavy queues will reduce end-user tail without significantly reducing overall throughput.
3) The combination of adaptive windowing + priority will outperform either alone on mixed workloads but may require careful fairness knobs to prevent starvation.

Experiment design overview:
- Three experiment arms (A/B/C):
  A) Baseline: current fixed timeout + FIFO batching.
  B) Adaptive windowing only.
  C) Adaptive windowing + priority queues.
- For each arm run paramized grid over: max_batch {8, 16, 32}, base_timeout_ms {8, 16, 32}, adaptive_sensitivity {0.1, 0.5, 1.0} (how quickly window shrinks/expands), and priority_threshold_window {true,false}.
- We will also run microbench profiling cases to isolate serialization, queue-lock contention, and KV cache hot paths.

Workloads (synthetic + captured traces):
1) Interactive-heavy: 80% small requests (<=64 tokens), 20% medium (65-512). Peak arrival bursts.
2) Mixed: 40% small, 40% medium, 20% long (>=1024). Poisson arrivals with occasional spikes.
3) Long-job dominated: 60% long, 40% medium; used to check throughput loss.
4) Production replay: anonymized sample of 24h traffic (off-peak subset) from hosted-api region-us-west.

Measurement metrics (primary/secondary):
- Primary: p50, p90, p95, p99, p999 latency (end-to-end request start->first-token and to completion), 99.9 tail is critical.
- Secondary: tokens/sec, GPU utilization, CPU in batching loop, batch formation latency (time from first request in batch to dispatch), queue wait times per-priority, fairness index (KL divergence of per-tenant latency distributions), cost estimate per 100k tokens.
- Microprofiling signals: mutex contention time, syscall counts, allocation rate in batching path, time spent serializing input/outputs, KV cache hits/misses during a request.

Instrumentation required:
- Add fine-grained timers around: enqueue, dequeue, batch-coalescing, serialization, runtime dispatch, post-dispatch cleanup.
- Expose per-request metadata: route, customer_tier, estimated_sequence_length, priority_tag.
- Sampling flamegraphs for batching worker threads at 1% sampling during runs.
- Export histograms to Prometheus and heatmaps to Grafana modal panels.

Profiling steps (microbench):
1) Run tight loop synthetic generator hitting batching loop only (no GPU) to measure queue and serialization overhead.
2) Run with model stub (zero-op forward) to emulate runtime dispatch without heavy GPU to separate scheduling vs compute.
3) Full-stack runs on a single-GPU node (with real model) to observe end-to-end latency and resource interaction.

Adaptive windowing algorithm (sketch):
- Maintain EWMA of inter-arrival time (IAT) per route-window.
- Compute target_window = clamp(k * EWMA, min_timeout, max_timeout). k is a tunable multiplier to bias latency vs throughput.
- When arrivals exceed batch fill rate, algorithm halves the window faster (multiplier alpha_up) and increases slower on decreases (alpha_down) to avoid oscillation.
- Safety: never shrink below minimal_timeout_ms to avoid starvation of low-throughput routes.

Priority queue behavior (sketch):
- Assign priority tier per request: interactive (high), normal (default), background (low).
- Maintain separate logical queues and allow prioritized harvesting into batches up to a max_fraction (e.g., 0.6 of slots) to protect throughput.
- If high-priority backlog exists, low-priority requests are deferred up to starvation_threshold_ms then forcibly included.

Acceptance criteria:
- Combined approach (C) must reduce p99 by >=20% on mixed workload vs baseline A without lowering tokens/sec by more than 5% on long-job dominated workload.
- No per-tenant fairness index regression beyond configured threshold (KL divergence <= 0.05 increase).
- CPU overhead in batching loop increases < 15% (acceptable), or we identify further optimization to compensate.

Run plan and timelines:
- Week 1: implement instrumentation and adaptive window prototype (branch: feat/adaptive-window).
- Week 2: implement prioritized queue prototype and safety knobs.
- Week 3: microbench profiling + synthetic workload runs.
- Week 4: production trace replay + extended runs for stability.
- Week 5: analyze, prepare Canary config and rollback plan, docs for Console toggles.

Safety and rollout considerations:
- Feature flags per-cluster and per-customer with quick rollback.
- Circuit-breaker: if p99 degraded beyond 30% for 5min, auto-disable and alert.
- Canary to 2% of traffic then 10% then 30% with health gates.

Risks and open questions:
- Priority schemes may be gamed by customers if priority can be inferred. Need enforcement at auth layer or rate-limits per-priority.
- Interaction between adaptive windowing and autoscaling: may create oscillations in observed arrival rates—need to coordinate signals.
- Memory/alloc pressure caused by holding more partial batches when window expands.

Unresolved items / TODOs:
- [ ] Choose default adaptive_sensitivity and k from small exploratory sweep.
- [ ] Add Prometheus labels for priority_tier and route in batching metrics.
- [ ] Draft runbook entry for rollback and customer communication.
- [ ] Create short demo video for Console showing priority toggles and observed p99 improvement.

Appendix: example experiment matrix (abridged)
- Arm B/C x max_batch {8,16} x base_timeout {8,16,32} x sensitivity {0.1,0.5} x workload {interactive,mixed}
- Estimated runs: ~150 distinct runs, each 20–40 minutes plus warmup. Total cluster time budget estimate: 8–12 node-days depending on concurrency.

Notes to self: keep logs of corner cases where a single long request holds the batch and forces long tail for small requests; we might need a per-request preemption or forced split. See linked PR for earlier preemption discussion.
